title: A Bird's Eye View of the World, for the centennial
creator: Daniel Vierge
description: Daniel Vierge, a notable Spanish illustrator working in Paris, created this centerfold view of a literal “World on Display” (as projected from outer space) as a supplement to the London Daily Graphic, a weekly illustrated newspaper, on the occasion of the opening of the Centennial Exposition in the United States. Published in French, this richly illustrated and handcolored view of the world encompasses geography, natural wonders, cultural diversity, and scientific and archaeological advancements made over thousands of years, including the Mayan and Aztec ruins in Mexico and the pyramids of Giza, Egypt. Also included, representing more recent innovations in travel and transportation are covered wagons and the Union Pacific Railroad in the United States (completed in 1869) and the transatlantic trade lines between New York and France. Vierge also featured 79 illustrations of people from around the world in traditional dress situated along the bottom border. For those who couldn’t travel to Philadelphia to witness America’s first foray into World’s Fairs and Expositions in person, Vierge’s illustrations hinted at the complicated narratives and overwhelming visuals competing for fairgoers’ attention  in each of the Fair’s Buildings and curated exhibits.

title: Plan of the City of Philadelphia, 1876 drawn and engraved by W.H. Gamble
creator: W.H. Gamble
description: This map displays all of Philadelphia and was created to commemorate the 100th anniversary of American Independence and the Centennial Exposition designed to celebrate that anniversary. Philadelphia is color-coded into several sections and numerous street grids and the map highlights Fairmount Park as the site where the Centennial Exposition was held. The map features eight illustrations of the Fair’s key buildings, including: the Main Building, Machinery Hall, Memorial Hall, Horticulture Hall, Agricultural Hall, the U.S. Government Building, the Womens’ Pavilion and Judges Hall. These detailed illustrations showcase the size of these buildings, and reflect the work of Exposition organizers to instill pride and patriotism. Several railroad lines and waterways are highlighted as well. The map functions as both a city plan as well as a commemorative piece for the fair. It also showcases Philadelphia’s role and sense of pride as one of the key cities at the center of American patriotism. Seeing the size of Fairmount Park puts into perspective the large-scale operation that this fair was. The map had both a utilitarian use (as a guide to the city and the exposition) and a sentimental use (as a keepsake or souvenir).

title: Centennial Exhibition : with a full description of the great buildings and all the objects of interest in them.
creator: National Publishing Co.
description:
This poster is an advertisement for a publication about the 1876 Centennial Exhibition. Designed to capture public interest, it promotes a richly illustrated book that serves as a comprehensive guide to the exhibition's buildings, displays, and attractions. Titled with large, festive lettering, the poster promotes the book’s vivid descriptions and detailed images of the great exhibition halls, including the Main Building, Machinery Hall, and Horticultural Hall.

This poster is a prime example of promotional material—it reflects the enthusiasm and optimism of post-Civil War America, and is overly eager to boast its industrial and cultural achievements to the world. It also reveals the troubling commercialization of historical memory at the center of World’s Fairs. Under the seemingly innocent narrative of a nation celebrating a civic milestone, the Centennial Exhibition was intended to be packaged as a consumer spectacle. These materials transformed a temporary public event into a commodified product, designed to be bought, collected, and displayed. In doing so, the publishers exploited patriotic sentiment to profit within a growing marketplace of souvenirs and mass-produced historical narratives. The result was that complex cultural and historical experiences were reduced to items of easy consumption.

Ultimately, this poster is not just a historical artifact of the Centennial, it is a reflection of how commercial interests dominate the shaping of public memory and national identity (in 1876 and today). It reveals the early stages of an intellectual shift in which history and “culture” were increasingly curated, packaged, and sold in ways that prioritized marketability over honest, critical and authentic engagement with peoples, places and objects that were collected and on display.
subject: Exhibition views
image_alt_text: Poster advertising the World Fair with images of some exhibits.

title: Souvenir map of the World's Columbian Exposition at Jackson Park and Midway Plaisance, Chicago, Ill., U.S.A., 1893
creator: Hermann Heinze
description: This map was produced as both a guide to the fair and a souvenir from the fair, and features a complete overview of the extensive fairgrounds and the mile-long Midway Plaisance. The Chicago Fair was the first fair to include a separate Midway entertainment area for amusements, and all subsequent fairs followed suit. The Maine State Building is visible on the map, just above the east annex of the Palace of Fine Arts. Ethnological villages, also referred to as “Human Zoos,”were present in both the Midway and around south pond “Ethno-Graphical Exhibit” (located just above the Anthropology building on this map). This map also helps us to understand how visitors traveled to and from the World’s Columbian Exposition, which was mainly by railroad. Fairgoers were also able to experience the world’s first electric elevated railway. The intramural or elevated electric road, operated within the grounds to help visitors navigate the massive Exposition. The system was about six miles in length and the full circuit was made in less than half an hour, which afforded an excellent view of the Exposition. The intramural road cost $1,000,000, and although 6,000,000 passengers rode the electric railway during the fair, it resulted in significant losses.

title: Bird's eye view of the World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago, 1893
description: Rand McNally’s large format bird’s-eye view map of the World’s Columbian Exposition provided an expansive aerial perspective of the fairgrounds in Chicago that captured the essence of a transformative era in American history. The view served not only as a practical guide for visitors attempting to navigate the vast exhibition but also as an artistic representation of the fair’s architectural and ideological splendor. Key buildings and pavilions at the fair, which included the Administration Building, Machinery Hall, and the Agricultural Building, are labeled and intricately illustrated. This detailed and intricate illustration work within the map showcased the dedication of fair organizers to emerging American ideals related to industrial progress and agricultural innovation. Various aspects of the fair’s design, such as waterways and lagoons, are highlighted within the map. These water features provided essential transportation routes for visitors and enhanced the overall aesthetic appeal of the grounds as they created a serene environment within the fairgrounds reminiscent of both European and Japanese gardens. Small boats within the lagoons added to the picturesque scene and invited attendees to explore the fair in a leisurely manner. The World’s Columbian Exposition symbolized a nation’s bold ambitions to demonstrate its power and cultural achievements to the world. This fair was more than just a showcase; it was an effort to assert national dominance. This map served as a testament to the vision of its creators, aiming to preserve the spirit of the fair for generations to come.

title: The Dream city, the World's Columbian Exhibition
description: This chromolithographic bird's-eye view illustrates the planned layout of the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago and aimed to showcase the Neoclassical and Beaux Art architectural designs of Daniel Burnham’s structures with their white faux-stone facades. In the background, the sprawling city of Chicago is visible, with smoke rising from numerous chimneys—an American symbol of industrial progress and prosperity at the turn-of-the-century. Elegant buildings line the formal avenues of the Exposition, while elaborate waterways flow through exhibition halls and gardens. At night, the scene was illuminated by electric lights, a rare sight in most American cities at the time. The lake is depicted as bustling with sailboats and steamships that transported passengers to and from the exhibition pier. Produced by the American Fine Art Company, this map was printed as a promotional souvenir for the World's Columbian Exposition. It captured the fair's image of order, power, and ambition, while also obscuring the realities of poverty, protest, and exclusion in an American landscape just beyond its borders. More than just a guide, the map reflects the visions that planners had for the future and highlights the complicated narratives of American progress those same planners chose to overlook.

title: The Great Exhibition of the Industry of all Nations , opened by her Majesty Queen Victoria
description: This view of the Great Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations, created by John Tallis, showcases a wide perspective of the 1851 Crystal Palace Exhibition in London, England. The 1851 Exhibition is quite significant as it marked the first of many World’s Fairs and Exhibitions of culture and industry in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. The Crystal Palace itself, illustrated here, was meant to showcase England’s architectural and industrial prowess. At 563 x 138 metres (1848 x 454 feet), and composed mostly of cast iron and glass, the Crystal Palace was a modern marvel. The structure housed numerous exhibitions and was temporarily placed in Hyde Park for the five-month duration of the fair. The Crystal Palace structure was disassembled after the fair and relocated to Sydenham Hill (located in south London) where it hosted subsequent exhibitions until it was destroyed by a fire in 1936. Tallis’ view illustrates the front facade of the Crystal Palace, the surrounding park, and large crowds of people, demonstrating the popularity of the first World’s Fair. Framed with gold adornments and coat of arms, the decorations display the British Crown’s prowess and pride in the structure and the exhibitions contained within its glass walls.

title: Exposition Universelle de Paris 1889
description: As a celebration of the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution, the Exposition Universelle de Paris 1889 underscored industrial and economic independence within France. This detailed print, a chromolithograph, frames the exhibition’s fairgrounds with postcard views, banners, and the flags of numerous participating countries. The banners feature mottos in French, English, and Latin, including "Pax" [Peace], "Agriculture," "Industry," "Travail" [Work],  “Arts,” and “Sciences.” In total, there are thirteen postcard views along the poster’s border, each focusing on different buildings, exhibitions, or experiences within the Exposition Universelle. These postcards shine a light on France’s growing empire and colonies in North Africa and Indochina, including “L’Arabie,” “Colonies Francises Annam,” and “Colonies Francaises - Tonkin,” displaying the breadth of France’s colonial, imperialistic reach. Specially constructed for the Exposition, Gustave Eiffel’s Tower stands high above the fairgrounds. This Chromolithograph also highlights the multiple exhibit buildings that housed what fair organizers deemed “technological advancements.” In the foreground of the image, a small train shuttles attendees around the fairgrounds as smoke billows out of its chimney–an almost universal symbol of “progress.”

title: Exposition de Universelle de 1900: plan d'ensemble rez-de-chaussee.
description: While dozens of new buildings and attractions had been built since Paris last hosted the Exposition Universelle in 1889, among the most significant innovations in the ensuing years were advances in electricity. Visitors to Paris, the “City of Light,” in 1900 were dazzled and overwhelmed by the electrification of the Exposition. Tens of thousands of incandescent bulbs lit the fair well into the evening, and the Eiffel Tower featured arc lighting that swept over the fairgrounds. One of the main attractions of the Fair was the Palais de l’électricité. Designed by Eugène Hénard, the building was entirely lit by and decorated with thousands of electrical bulbs inside and out. The inside of the Palais had a mirror system that multiplied the sources of light, adding to the magic of the experience, and the exterior of the building was crowned by a chariot drawn by hippogriffs spewing showers of multi-coloured flames each evening. This intricate printed map of the Exposition, with dozens of manuscript notations, shows the overall schematics for the high voltage cables, circuits, and connections that made the electrification of the fair possible, a significant feat that required careful coordination and considerable resources. The fairytale spectacle of illumination obscured and distorted the realities of colonization, imperialism, and the darker sides of France’s industrial prowess.

title: Panorama from the moving boardwalk
creator: Thomas A. Edison, Inc
description: This short, yet insightful film gives modern viewers a glimpse into the world of the 1900 Paris Exposition. A very early example of the “moving picture,” the Edison Manufacturing Company sought to record and create films showcasing the technological advancements on display and in use at the Exposition, and sent producer James H. White to Paris to capture the fair. Adults and children can be seen jumping on and off the boardwalk as it whisks people away to other areas of the fairgrounds. The moving boardwalk made its first debut at the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893 in Chicago, Illinois. Impressed with the capability to transport people quickly around the exposition, France recreated the moving boardwalk in 1900.  Interestingly, the French referred to it as the “Paris trottoir roulant” and the “Rue de l’Avenir” [street of the future], even though the technology had been around for nearly a decade. The boardwalk was designed by American architect Joseph Lyman Silsbee and American engineer Max E. Schmidt. According to the New York Observer, the boardwalk featured three elevated platforms: the first one was stationary, the second moved at a moderate speed, and the third moved at almost 6 miles per hour, a wholly novel experience for millions of fairgoers.

title: Scene from the elevator ascending Eiffel Tower
creator: Thomas A. Edison, Inc
description: Construction began on the Eiffel Tower in 1887 and was completed  just two months before the opening of the 1889 Paris World’s Fair. The tower was built with the intention of creating a 300-metre-tall structure to commemorate the 1889 Exposition Universelle, which celebrated the centennial of the French Revolution. The Tower was designed by Gustave Eiffel, an entrepreneur and engineer whose proposed design was selected from 107 submissions. Despite the heavy criticism of Eiffel’s design, and opposition from several large names in the Paris art world, the tower was completed in just two and a half years. This was a significant feat for the time as it took four people to install each of the rivets that hold the tower together (there are about 2,500,000 rivets in total). Edison’s brief moving picture, filmed at the 1900 Paris Fair, demonstrates the sheer height of the tower which, at the time of completion, was the tallest building in the world. The elevators featured in the film pushed the boundaries of height and capacity that lifts had previously been able to achieve. Fairgoers from across the world came to visit the Eiffel tower and experience the capabilities of the elevators to the top. The tower welcomed 2,000,000+ visitors over the six month duration of the 1900 Paris World’s Fair.
subject: Exhibition views
source: Library of Congress Motion Picture, Broadcasting and Recorded Sound Division

title: Vue Panoramique de l'Exposition Universelle de 1900
creator: Lucien Baylac
description: This panoramic view was produced for the 1900 Exposition Universelle, a World's Fair held in Paris, France, to celebrate the achievements of the past century and usher in the new one. The map presents a bird’s eye view of the fairgrounds along the Seine, including iconic temporary structures built for the Exposition, including the Palais de l’Electricite, the Grand Palais, and the moving boardwalk that transported visitors between exhibition zones. Designed both as a functional navigational tool and as a souvenir, Baylac’s view reflects the fair’s blend of art, science, and spectacle. It offers a compelling visual summary of an event that welcomed over 50 million visitors and showcased innovations such as escalators, moving pictures, and early developments in what we now label “public transit.” The style and color choices reflect the Art Nouveau aesthetic that defined much of the fair’s visual culture. Art Nouveau, an international art and design movement that began in France, flourished from the late-ninteenth century into the early-twentieth century. Translated as “New Art,” the popular artistic movement was known by different names across Europe such as Jugendstil in Germany and Stile Liberty in Italy.

title: Sights, scenes and wonders at the World's fair; official book of views of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition. Reproduced from Goerz lens photographs
creator: Louisiana Purchase Exposition (1904 : Saint Louis, Mo.)
description: This photograph, included in a souvenir booklet and titled “Chiefs and Squaws in Native Costume,” provides a window into the demeaning representations of Native Americans at the St. Louis World’s Fair, and specifically, in this instance, for the eight individual Native men and women who were being collectively referred to as “Chiefs” and “Squaws.” Both of these terms, considered offensive today, were used in 1904 to reduce the complexities of Native peoples and then amplified to give fairgoers a superficial experience with the peoples in the photograph. If you look at the bottom of the photograph, the subtitle indicates that these eight individuals were all members of Buffalo Bill’s Wild West Show, the Indian Congress, and Rough Riders of the World. These titles are congruent with the fair’s themes of victory and conquest following the United States’ victory over Spain in the Spanish-American War in 1898. Native American presence in the Wild West period is commonly associated with resistance to westward expansion, as well as the U.S. Government’s policies that ripped Native peoples from their lands. Like the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, the Indian Congress exhibited the many different ways of Native life and cultures, gathering members from 35 different tribes.
subject: Exhibition views; Guidebook; Ethnography
image_alt_text: Souvenir book for the World's Fair.

title: The Rhode Island building : Louisiana Purchase Exposition, St. Louis, 1904
description: One of the most interesting aspects of this souvenir booklet from the Rhode Island Building are the advertisements in the back of the booklet, which reveal a good deal about consumption patterns in early-twentieth century America. The advertisement for “Santinas Plumbing Fixtures,” shown here, was created by the Smith & Anthony Company. This advertisement reflected America’s push to make technological innovation, public health, and domestic sanitation central to the American vision of progress. For many fair visitors, the World’s Fair bathrooms were their first look at the future of indoor plumbing. These amenities were featured to demonstrate to fairgoers the pretense of “superior” modern technology to Native American ways of life and being. Other advertisements in Rhode Island’s official fair book demonstrated the eagerness of the United States to flaunt its growing industries. This ad for ginger ale connected everyday products such as ginger ale, a popular soda at the time, with national pride and sent the message that American goods could compete and win on a global stage. The St. Louis World’s Fair served as an important stage for promoting American exceptionalism on the smaller scale of common household products. This nationalistic mindset crept into the everyday lives of the average American through products like ginger ale and kitchen appliances. The United States was determined to prove they were the best in every category, even soda.

title: Geronimo, the famous Apache chieftain, for many years a terror to the early settlers, Worlds Fair, St. Louis, 1904
creator: William H. Rau
description:
“In St. Louis, everyone with a camera and a little money could shoot and capture Geronimo, performing a personal colonization on a private scale.”

~ James R. Swensen, Bound for the Fair

William J. McGee, the principal of the St. Louis Fair’s Department of Anthropology, organized an anthropological exhibition that contained the most comprehensive display of living Native Americans. Of all the “surviving chiefs” of the many tribal nations that McGee wished to display at the fair, only Geronimo, the leader of the Chiricahua Apache, agreed to make an appearance. The public opinion of Geronimo was that he was nefarious.

Viewed as a ruthless, animalistic “savage,” Geronimo’s presence was not just a spectacle for onlookers; fairgoers were permitted to approach and interact with him intimately. The exhibit was marketed as an opportunity for visitors to experience the stories of his raids and subsequent capture for themselves; many photographs of Geronimo were produced for this purpose.

In reality, however, McGee was the nefarious one. His reason for showcasing Geronimo’s presence at the fair was to celebrate American processes to ethnically cleanse and erase Native ways of being. In collaboration with Samuel McCowan, the director of the fair’s Model Indian School (pictured here), the exhibit sought to demonstrate the “positive” effects of assimilating Native Americans. On one side of the school, Geronimo and other older Native artisans made traditional crafts. This portrayal of Geronimo juxtaposed the presences of younger Native children on the other side of the school who were forcibly taught to speak English and assimilate to an American education, like their counterparts at the Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania, who also sponsored an exhibit at the Fair. This pitting of Geronimo (as an Indian artisan) against Native children (as people “saved” by American education) allowed white fairgoers to view the “Indian transformation” in real time. Native Americans were used as (literal) props to demonstrate the illusion that modern technology was superior to Native ways of life, but this came at a greater expense: the erasure of Native cultures, languages, and practices.
subject: Ethnography; Exhibition views
source: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division

title: Largest locomotive in the world, weighs 239 tons, used in B.Y.O. Freight Service, Transportation Building, Worlds Fair, St. Louis, 1904.
creator: William H. Rau
description:
Some of the most advertised aspects of the St. Louis World’s Fair were displays of American innovation and industrialization. Festival Hall was one of the central locations for these sorts of displays. It faced the eight main palaces and was a testament to technological advances of the time. At night the building and surrounding water features were completely illuminated, a stunning sight for many Americans visiting the fair who had never seen this type of light show. Decorative plates depicting an image of Festival Hall and Cascade Gardens could be purchased as souvenirs (see the example below) and engraved with your name. Directly facing Festival hall were the most important buildings of the fair, which included the Palaces of Electricity, Machinery, Transportation, and Manufacturing. Within these exhibit buildings the latest examples of technology were displayed, from the “largest locomotive in the world” showcasing the might of American railroads in the transportation building to a wireless telegraph tower in the Palace of Electricity.

New point and shoot cameras were also one of these latest technologies available at the fair. Personal cameras had recently become available to the public and were heavily used at the fair. However, not just anyone was allowed to take pictures! Photography licenses were issued by anthropologists who were involved in organizing the fair – a prime example of how anthropology and anthropologists controlled the fair’s narratives and themes. Within the boundaries of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition the United States wanted to cement its reputation as a world power and usher in a “new age” of innovation and progress. However, those ideas of progress were often flawed and came at the expense of Native American and other Indigenous ways of life. Throughout the Fair, Indigenous peoples were seen as people of the past with no place in the “New” America of railroads and western expansion that the United States government was selling to the world. The St. Louis World’s Fair perpetuated harmful ideas about Native American peoples that attempted to excuse their genocide–the purposeful erasure of Native lives and complexities–as a by-product of progress.
subject: Exhibition views
source: Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division

title: Souvenir of Pan-American exposition : Buffalo, May 1 to November 1, 1901
creator: Robert Reid
description: These souvenir booklets would have been purchased during the fair as keepsakes to take home. Pictured here is the West Pavilion of the 410 foot tall “Electric Tower,” lit by 40,000 electric lamps and featuring a fountain with water torrenting out of the center (sourced and redirected from Niagara Falls) and flanked by two statue groups by the sculptor George Gray Barnard  “Great Waters in the Days of the White Man” and “Great Waters in the Days of the Red Man.” The Niagara water then traveled through the hydro-electric generator that was able to power the electric lights for the entire Exposition. At the turn-of-the- century, one of the biggest motivations behind having world’s fairs was to show off new innovations and emerging, marvelous concepts to the general population. Even though the Electric Tower was a temporary building, for a guest to come to the fair and see electricity for perhaps the first time must have been a very memorable occasion. This lighting up of Buffalo during the fair was made possible by the exploitation of the Great Lakes and Niagara Falls, equating water with white progress over and above traditional Indigenous practices, with electricity spawning a continual spreading of ideas of “progress” and human interactions.
subject: Exhibition views
image_alt_text: Souvenir photobook from the Pan-American Exposition.

title: Official Souvenir Mailing Card: Ethnology Building
description: The ornate Renaissance-style Ethnology building was built by local Buffalo architect George Cary. The contents within this building, like in all U.S. Government-sponsored exhibits at the Fair were coordinated and curated by the Smithsonian Institution. The Anthropological and Archeological displays within the building exhibited what the Smithsonian’s white curators believed were the "cultures," "ways of life," and "evolution" of non-white American and non-European peoples. These white curators were harmful in their exhibits. For example, the artist of the postcard included a canoe and teepee in the foreground, despite the fact that the Seneca Nation, the Native peoples whose land Buffalo stole, lived in longhouses not teepees. This inclusion of what is wrong and exclusion of what is correct highlights the overall treatment of Indigenous peoples at the Buffalo Exposition. Cultural exhibits were used as performance pieces that often cemented Native peoples within a theater of the past. The entirety of the fair was used to remind white Americans of their supposed superior place in the timeline of “progress,” while Native voices were excluded from the conversation. This intentionality is supported by this postcard which was likely mass-produced as a snapshot souvenir representing the Ethnology Building at fair, whose exhibits were designed without Native input.
subject: Exhibition views
image_alt_text: Postcard with image of the Ethnology Building from the Pan American Exposition.

title: Pan-American Exposition, Buffalo, N.Y., U.S.A., 1901
creator: Raphael Beck
description:
“The Emblem has been most effectively utilized as an advertisement for the Exposition … It was reproduced in three colors on cards 3 by 5 ins. and printed in vast quantities, the total number being 2,296,579. These cards were issued in English, Spanish, French, and Portuguese, and circulated throughout the world. It was also reproduced in large size - nine inches in diameter - for hangers, of which over 100,000 were distributed. The hangers were lithographed in nine colors and were particularly attractive. Referring to them, a prominent railroad official recently said that their use was the ‘greatest piece of advertising work he had seen since the Centennial Exposition at Philadelphia twenty-four years ago.’”

-The Profitable Advertiser, 1901

The logo for the Pan-American Exposition was designed by New York artist Raphael Beck, whose design was selected by the Pan-American Exposition Commission in 1899 from over 400 entries. In the logo, North America (wearing the red phyringian liberty cap) and South America (sporting the star of empire) are personified as women. Beck’s models for the Americas were Maude Colemen Woods and Maxine Eliot, recently declared the winners of the New York World’s “most representatively beautiful women in America” contest (also chosen from hundreds of entries). It is notable within the logo that the representation of both continents for a fair that promoted the independence and growth of nations in the Western Hemisphere were portrayed as white women from the United States, and did not also include an actual representation of the millions of Indigenous, Black, and Latinx women of color on both continents.

creator: Thomas A. Edison, Inc
description: From the 1850s to the 1900s, World's Fair and Exhibitions were political games. They were organized so that the nation hosting them could turn curiosities and exhibitions of new technologies into a strong affirmation of their dominance over everything. But there were also games within the game. As the United States shifted from genocidal work across its continent to the safety and leisure of the World's Fair, organizers of World's Fair Exhibitions in the United States wanted to send veiled messages to the public that the Indigenous peoples that they continued to suppress (inside and outside the Fairgrounds) were willing to participate in their own dematerialization and humiliation. In this particular scene from the Buffalo Exposition in 1901, in a stadium that might remind you of the Roman Coliseum, 250+ American Indian (Indigenous) peoples were made to act out scenes of battle against White men dressed as soldiers. This theatrical transformation of American Indian peoples from political sovereigns to caricatures on a field of play helped set the stage for the next century of American Indian peoples as mascots, team names and caricatures on football, basketball, baseball, lacrosse, soccer and other sports fields.
